questions.q: A particle is projected up from a point at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal direction. At any time $t$, if $p$ is the linear momentum, $y$ is the vertical displacement, $x$ is horizontal displacement, the graph among the following which does not represent the variation of kinetic energy KE of the particle is
questions.solution:
Momentum, $p=m \cdot v \Rightarrow v=\left(\frac{p}{m}\right)$
Kinetic energy, KE \begin{array}{l} =\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{p^{2}}{m^{2}}\right)=\frac{1}{2 m} p^{2} \\ \text { or, } \mathrm{KE} \propto p^{2} \quad\left(\because \frac{1}{2 m}=\text { constant }\right) \end{array} Hence, the graph between $\mathrm{KE}$ and $p^{2}$ will be linear. Now, kinetic energy $\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$ The velocity component at point $P$, $v_{y}=(u \sin \theta-g t)$ and $v_{x}=u \cos \theta$ Resultant velocity at point $P$ \begin{aligned} \vec{v} &=v_{y} \hat{j}+v_{x} \hat{i} \\ &=(u \sin \theta-g t) \hat{j}+u \cos \theta \hat{i} \\ &|\vec{v}|=\sqrt{(u \cos \theta)^{2}+(u \sin \theta-g t)^{2}} \\ =\sqrt{u^{2} \cos ^{2} \theta+u^{2} \sin ^{2} \theta+g^{2} t^{2}-2 u g t \sin \theta} \\ &=\sqrt{u^{2}\left(\cos ^{2} \theta+\sin ^{2} \theta\right)+g^{2} t^{2}-2 u g t \sin \theta} \end{aligned} \therefore \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(u^{2}+g^{2} t^{2}-2 u g t \sin \theta\right)ii/ i. e., $\mathrm{KE} \propto t^{2}$ Hence, graph will be parabolic intercept on $y$-axis. Hence, the graph between $\mathrm{KE}$ and $t$. Now, in case of height \begin{array}{l} \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(v^{2}\right) \text { and } v^{2}=\left(u^{2}-2 g y\right) \\ \therefore \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(u^{2}-2 g y\right) \\ \mathrm{KE}=-m g y+\frac{1}{2} m u^{2} \end{array} Intercept on $y$-axis $=\frac{1}{2} m u^{2}$
\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{x}{t}\right)^{2} i.e., $\mathrm{KE} \propto x^{2}$. Thus graph between $\mathrm{KE}$ and $x$ will be parabolic.

The train which is moving along the direction of rotation of earth that is west to east, will require less centripetal force compared to train moving in opposite direction.

Since the centripetal force is more on the train which move along the direction of rotation of earth therefore the normal reaction acting on the train will be more.

The surface is now tilted to an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal and the same block is made to go up on the surface with the same initial velocity $v$. The decrease in the mechanical energy in the second situation is smaller than that in the first situation.
Statement II The coefficient of friction between the block and the surface decreases with the increase in the angle of inclination.
options: Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is a correct explanation for Statement I
Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is NOT a correct explanation for Statement I
Statement I is true, Statement II is false
Statement I is false, Statement II is true

In statement I Decrease in mechanical energy in case I will be
$\Delta U_1=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$
But decrease in mechanical energy in case II will be
$\begin{aligned}
& \Delta U_2=\frac{1}{2} m v^2-m g h \\
& \Delta U_2 < \Delta U_1
\end{aligned}\therefore \quad \Delta U_2 < \Delta U_1$
or Statement $\mathrm{I}$ is correct.
In Statement II Coefficient of friction will not change or this Statement is wrong.
$\therefore$ Option (c) is correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements $A$ and $B$ identify the correct answer given below :
(A) A body initially at rest is acted upon by a constant force. The rate of change of its kinetic energy varies linearly with time
(B) When a body is at rest, it must be in equilibrium.
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2} m(a t)^2=\frac{1}{2} m a^2 t^2$
Rate of change of KE,
$\frac{d K}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{1}{2} m a^2 t^2\right)=m a^2 t\therefore \quad \frac{d K}{d t} \propto t$
So, statement $A$ is correct.
When the body is at rest, then it may be or may not be in equilibrium, so statement $B$ is wrong.

questions.q:
Statement (I) : The slope of kinetic energy-displacement curve of a body in motion will be directly proportional to its acceleration.

Statement (II) : From a height of $15 \mathrm{~m}$ a ball is projected vertically upwards with a velocity of $30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. If the ball rises to the same height after hitting the ground, the loss of its energy on hitting the ground is $30 \%$.
Statement (III) : The velocity acquired by a body of mass ' $m$ ' after travelling a fixed distance from rest under the action of a constant force is directly proportional to mass ' $\mathrm{m}$ '. 
Which of the following is correct?
options: Statements I, II, III are true
Statements I, III are true, but statement II is false
Statement I is true, but statements II and III are false
Statements I, II are true, but statement III is false
questions.solution:
We have
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV}^2 \\
& \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{dx}}(\mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E})=\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{m} \times 2 \mathrm{~V} \frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{dx}}
\end{aligned}$
Slope of $($ K.E $-\mathrm{x})$ curve $=\mathrm{ma} \propto \mathrm{a}$
So, (I) is correct
When ball just strike the ground, then
$\mathrm{V}=\sqrt{30^2+2 \times 10 \times 15}=\sqrt{1200} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
If ball reaches the same height after striking the ground then, velocity after collision $=30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\begin{aligned}
& \text { So, } \Delta \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}(1200-900) \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \times 300 \\
& \frac{\Delta \mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{E}} \times 100=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \times 300}{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \times 1200} \times 100=25 \%
\end{aligned}$
So, (II) is incorrect.
Now, equation of motion are independent of mass. So velocity will not depend on mass. So (III) is incorrect.

questions.solution:
Spring force follows Hooke's law \(F=-k x\).
Work done by spring depends only on initial and final positions, not the path \(\rightarrow\) so it is conservative.
For conservative forces, we can define a potential energy function (\(U=\frac{1}{2} k x^2\)).
Hence, spring force is conservative because potential energy is defined only for conservative forces.

questions.q:

(B) Work done by gravitational force in lifting a bucket out of a well by a rope tied to the bucket is negative

(C) Work done by friction on a body sliding down an inclined plane is positive

(D) Work done by an applied force on a body moving on a rough horizontal plane with uniform velocity is zero

(E) Work done by the air resistance on an oscillating pendulum is negative

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Work done is given by, W=Fscosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement.

case(A): Direction of force and displacement both are in the same direction and hence work done will be positive. Hence, wrong.

case(B): Direction of force and displacement both are in the opposite direction and hence work done will be negative. Hence, correct.

case(C): Direction of force and displacement both are in the opposite direction and hence work done will be negative. Hence, wrong.

case(D): Direction of force and displacement both are in the same direction and hence work done will be positive. Hence, wrong.

case(E): Direction of force and displacement both are in the opposite direction and hence work done will be negative. Hence, correct.

\text{(B) Displacement is proportional to} & \text{(q) } t^2 \\
\text{(C) Work done is proportional to} & \text{(r) } t^3 \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
\(P \propto t\)
\(W=\int P d t=\int \alpha t d t \quad \text { or } \quad W \propto t^2\)
Since, work done is equal to change is KE
Hence, \(\quad v^2 \propto t^2\) or \(v \propto t\)
Further, \(\quad v=\frac{d s}{d t}\)
\(\therefore \quad \frac{d s}{d t} \propto t \quad \text { or } \quad d s \propto t d t\)
or \(s \propto t^2\) (by integration)

A block of mass \(m\) is stationary with respect to a rough wedge as shown in figure. Starting from rest in time \(t\), (\(m=1 \mathrm{~kg}, \theta=30^{\circ}, a=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2, t=4 \mathrm{~s}\)) work done on block
\(\begin{array}{l|l} \text{Column I} & \text{Column II} \\ \hline \text { (A) By gravity } & \text { (p) } 144 \mathrm{~J} \\ \text { (B) By normal reaction } & \text { (q) } 32 \mathrm{~J} \\ \text { (C) By friction } & \text { (r) } 56 \mathrm{~J} \\ \text { (D) By all the forces } & \text { (s) } 48 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \text { (t) } \text { None } \\ \hline \end{array}\)
options: \(A \rightarrow p, B \rightarrow t, C \rightarrow s, D \rightarrow q\)
\(A \rightarrow t, B \rightarrow p, C \rightarrow s, D \rightarrow q\)
\(A \rightarrow s, B \rightarrow p, C \rightarrow p, D \rightarrow q\)
\(A \rightarrow q, B \rightarrow p, C \rightarrow s, D \rightarrow t\)
questions.solution:
\(\begin{aligned} & \text { In } t=4 \mathrm{~s}, \\ & \nu=a t=8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \text { and } s =\frac{1}{2} a t^2=16 \mathrm{~m} \\ & \mathrm{KE} =\frac{1}{2} m v^2=32 \mathrm{~J} \end{aligned}\) From work-energy theorem, Work done by all the forces \(=\Delta \mathrm{KE}=32 \mathrm{~J}\) \(\begin{aligned} & \text {Work done by gravity }=-m g h =-(1)(10)(16) \\ & =-160 \mathrm{~J} \end{aligned}\) Writing equation of motion, we have, \(\Sigma F_y=m a\)
\(\begin{array}{lrl} N \cos 30^{\circ}+f \sin 30^{\circ}-10=m a & =2 \\ \text {or } & \sqrt{3} N+f & =24 \quad \ldots (i) \\ & \Sigma F_x & =0 \\ \therefore & N \sin 30^{\circ} & =f \cos 30^{\circ} \\ \text {or } & N & =\sqrt{3} f \quad \ldots (ii) \end{array}\) Solving Eqs. (i) and (ii), we have \(f=6 \mathrm{~N}\) \(\begin{aligned} & \text{and } N =\frac{18}{\sqrt{3}}=6 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~N} \\ & \text{Now, } W_N =(N \cos \theta)(s) \\ & =(6 \sqrt{3})\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(16)=144 \mathrm{~J} \\ W_F & =(f \sin \theta)(s) \\ & =(6) \frac{1}{2}(16)=48 \mathrm{~J} \end{aligned}\)
